items.title: 12.1 Structure and properties of the nucleus

source_refs.note: Topic 12.1 with the chapter's opening paragraph (PDF 262, printed 259). The learning objectives (PDF 261) are not reproduced.

blocks.text: We believe that all atoms are made up of neutrons, protons and electrons. The antiparticles of these three particles are also known. The positron (a positive electron), the neutrino and the photon are also known. By the end of the 1960s many new types of particles similar to the neutron and the proton had been discovered; these were called mesons, whose masses were mostly less than nucleon masses but more than the electron mass. Afterwards, other mesons were found with masses greater than nucleons. Physicists began to look for more fundamental particles, smaller constituents, which were later confirmed by experiments and named quarks. This chapter discusses the basic building blocks of matter.

The atomic nucleus comprises two types of particles: protons and neutrons. A proton is the nucleus of the simplest atom, hydrogen, called protium. The proton has a positive charge of the same magnitude as that of the electron (1.6 x 10^-19 C), and its mass is 1.67 x 10^-27 kg. The neutron, whose existence was pointed out in 1932 by James Chadwick, is electrically neutral, as its name suggests, and its mass is nearly the same as that of the proton. The two types of particles in the nucleus, neutrons and protons, are called nucleons.

A hydrogen nucleus consists of a single proton; the nuclei of all other elements consist of both neutrons and protons. The different nuclei are called nuclides. The number of protons in a nucleus is called the atomic number, Z. The total number of nucleons, the sum of neutrons and protons, is represented by A and called the atomic mass number, or simply mass number. The neutron number is N = A - Z ... (12.1). To specify a nucleus, the symbol X is written with A as a superscript and Z as a subscript before it, where X is the chemical symbol of the element.

blocks.title: Unified mass unit
blocks.text: To express the masses of atomic particles, instead of the kilogram, the unified mass scale (u) is generally used. By definition 1 u is exactly one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom: 1 u = 1.6606 x 10^-27 kg (equivalent to 931 MeV). In this unit the mass of a proton is 1.007276 u, that of a neutron 1.008665 u and that of an electron 0.00055 u.

blocks.title: Isotopes
blocks.text: Nuclei that contain the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes. Carbon nuclei always have 6 protons but may have 6, 7 or 8 neutrons: the isotopes of carbon are carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14. Among them carbon-12 and carbon-13 are stable, but carbon-14 is unstable and decays into nitrogen with the emission of beta and neutrino particles.

blocks.long_description: A nucleus is made of protons and neutrons, the nucleons; the number of protons is the atomic number, the total number of nucleons the mass number, and isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Four forces act in nature: the strong force, the strongest but reaching only across a nucleus; the electromagnetic force, about a hundredth as strong and long-ranged; the weak force, responsible for beta decay; and gravity, far the weakest. A gamma photon of at least 1.02 MeV passing near a nucleus can turn into an electron and a positron, and an electron meeting a positron can vanish into two gamma photons of 0.51 MeV each, with charge, momentum and energy conserved.
